# Checks that are known to fail, and the issue that will close each one.
#
# A check listed here is reported as `xfail` and does not fail the job. A check
# listed here that starts passing is reported as `XPASS` and does fail the job,
# so a fix cannot land without this file being updated in the same breath. That
# is the whole point: without it, either the run is permanently red and a new
# regression hides in the noise, or the known bugs get quietly dropped from the
# harness and stop being tracked at all.
#
# Columns: id, platform, issue number, note.
# Platform is one of: all, unix, windows, linux, macos.


# `cli/service/recovers macos 104` is back, and what 0.22.0 learned trying to
# remove it is worth more than the row.
#
# The theory was that the check could tell a host that cannot supervise from one
# that can, and skip rather than xfail. Two probes were tried on real runners.
# `launchctl print gui/<uid>` answers on the GitHub macOS runner, so the check
# ran and failed. `launchctl managername` returns "Aqua" there too, so it ran and
# failed again. The runner presents every property a real login session has and
# still will not bring a killed agent back.
#
# So there is no cheap probe, and a row here is the honest instrument until
# someone finds the real distinguishing property or the runner changes. The
# failure path already prints launchd's own words — see `c_service_recovers` —
# so the log says why rather than only that.

cli/service/recovers macos 104 the GitHub macOS runner reports an Aqua session and a gui domain and still does not keep a user agent alive; two probes for it were tried in 0.22.0 and both said the runner could supervise, measured working on real hardware in ~2s
